source.title: Individual Parameters in Weight-Sparse Transformers Appear Interpretable

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies whether individual weights in sparse transformers can be assigned input-context explanations. Its neuron case studies do not test how common neuron-level polysemanticity is or whether the mixed responses in the claim share a feature.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many results about per-weight interpretability, using conditional-zero ablations and LLM-generated predicates. Those results measure weight-level explanations, not neuron-level polysemanticity, so they are not cataloged as results for the claim versions. The Drori-sparse neuron case study is recorded as a related but different finding. Cited work on SoLU and other studies is not treated as this paper's result.
record.test_reason: The study measures whether individual weights in sparse and dense transformers have held-out explanations of when ablating them matters. It reports no rate of neuron polysemanticity in any model and no comparison of neuron polysemanticity across architectures or training regimes. Its neuron case studies (Gao digit neuron 1863, quote neurons 863/2790, Drori neuron 2461) are single examples read as single-concept detectors at the activation level, then decomposed into weight-level sub-roles. This is a related but different construct. Superposition and SoLU appear only in the introduction and related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one correction. The authors call the dense-model fraction of interpretable weights nearly zero (robust 1.5% and 0.4%), not merely much smaller. They also say the cross-model ordering survives changes in threshold, LLM and candidate budget, and that interpretability rises with a weight's causal impact. They present the neuron case studies as showing that single-label activation summaries hide parallel weight-level roles.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses per-weight ablation, conditional-zero scoring, and LLM-generated token-context predicates; it does not apply the neuron-level methods or measures in the claim's original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that its weight-interpretability rates vary with score threshold, candidate budget, and auto-interpretation LLM. These are sensitivities of its weight-level pipeline, not tests of claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: For one Drori-sparse MLP neuron, the activation-level profile reads as a single speech-verb detector. The 20 analyzed input weights are assigned five different functional roles.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-level neuron summaries can conceal multiple distinct functional roles among the neuron's input weights.

fits_no_version.finding: Gao-sparse digit neuron 1863 fires on numeric tokens. Each of its nine nonzero input weights gets its own predicate, falling into digit-count categories (Section 5, Figure 7, Table 3). Quote neurons 863 and 2790 are decomposed similarly (Figure 17). No rows record these.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In weight-sparse transformers, single-concept neurons are composed of input weights that each gate a narrower sub-case of the concept.

fits_no_version.finding: Robust per-weight interpretability rates: Gao sparse 15.0%, Drori sparse 9.6%, Drori dense 1.5%, Pythia-70m 0.4% (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-sparse training makes individual nonzero weights far more interpretable than weights in dense models.

record.problems: The neuron-level example is a single case study, and the weight decomposition profiles only the 20 highest-max-KL of 86 nonzero input weights; 66 weights are not analyzed. The paper's principal quantitative results concern weight interpretability rather than neuron polysemanticity.
record.rows_left_out: The pooled weight-interpretability rates, threshold and pipeline sweeps, and other per-weight results are omitted because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity. No results were omitted due to the row limit.

untested.parts: No share of polysemantic MLP neurons is reported, overall or by layer.
Superposition is invoked only as motivation from cited work; it is not tested as a cause.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
Sparse and dense models are compared on weight interpretability rates (Table 1), not on the share of polysemantic neurons. No neuron-level measure is reported for either.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
Threshold, LLM and candidate-budget sensitivity are reported only for weight-level scores, not for neuron polysemanticity judgments.

record.verdict_notes: Relation 'discusses' and tranche T6 are kept: superposition and SoLU are discussed in the introduction and related work, but none of the study's own results measure neuron polysemanticity. The Gao digit and quote neuron case studies are not recorded as rows and are not declared in rows_left_out. They bear on no version, so they are logged under fits_no_version rather than missing.

versions.untested_parts: The share of transformer MLP neurons with unrelated responses, including variation across layers.
Whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Whether neuron polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Changes in neuron polysemanticity due to activation function, architecture, or regularization, and effects on performance.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons have one shared feature or related jobs, or whether unrelated mixtures are rare.
Whether neuron polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range or explanation scoring.

rows.subject: Drori (2026), sparse
rows.operation_detail: Measured activation contexts for layer-1 MLP pre-GELU neuron 2461 on SimpleStories.

conditions.value: five sampled from each top-95% activation band

rows.value: Positive activations concentrated on speech verbs; negative activations dominated by copulas is and are.
rows.note: The authors characterize the activation-level pattern as a speech-verb detector. This single-neuron case study does not measure neuron-level polysemanticity prevalence or establish whether the responses are unrelated.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. This is a single-neuron qualitative profile: positive on speech verbs, negative pre-GELU on copulas. The authors call it one speech-verb detector. It gives no polysemanticity rate, and the negative tail is not a distinct positive response.

rows.subject: Drori (2026), sparse
rows.operation_detail: Profiled the 20 highest-max-KL input weights of neuron 2461 and assigned functional roles from their predicates.

conditions.value: top 20 of 86 nonzero input weights; remaining 66 not analyzed

rows.value: Five role clusters: speech-verb activators, mental-verb suppressors, a modal-verb suppressor, punctuation gates, and specific-token gates. Some individual weights passed the stated interpretability threshold; others did not.
rows.note: The result concerns roles of individual weights within one neuron, not whether that neuron's own responses constitute unrelated meanings.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The row covers the roles of the neuron's input weights, not the neuron's own responses. Only the top 20 of 86 nonzero input weights are profiled; the authors say the other 66 are below the noise floor.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
